title: Detection of Virtual Private Server
summary: This strategy detects Virtual Private Server, the resource development technique in which an adversary rents cloud compute from a commercial provider to use as operational infrastructure. It matters less as a direct intrusion signal and more as context: a virtual private server gives the attacker a stable, paid for, reputable looking address for command and control, phishing pages, and proxy hops, and it can be stood up and discarded in minutes. Detection relies on billing and cost anomaly reports for unexpected compute spend, cloud audit logs for instances created by new payment profiles or identities, authentication logs showing logons from hosting provider address ranges, and threat intelligence mapping of known hosting networks. It fails often because employees legitimately rent cloud servers for labs and projects, so finance visibility and identity correlation matter more than the resource itself.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for rented cloud servers used as attack infrastructure. A virtual private server is a computer you rent by the hour from a cloud company. The detection looks for connections from such servers and for unusual cloud spending in your own accounts.
beginner.whyItMatters: Rented servers are cheap, quick, and easy to throw away. Attackers use them to hide their real location and to keep a steady base. Their addresses often look clean, so blocklists do not stop them. Seeing that traffic arrive tells you an operation is active. Seeing unexpected spending tells you someone may be using your own cloud account.
howItWorks: Authentication and firewall logs record the address of every remote connection.
Address ranges are matched against known hosting and cloud provider networks.
The rule scores logons from those ranges when they target remote access services.
Cost reports flag new compute spending that no budget or project owns.
Cloud audit logs show instances created by identities or payment profiles not seen before.
Matches are combined with failure counts and account sensitivity before alerting.
beginner.example: Think of a van parked outside a bank every morning. The van is legal, the driver has done nothing wrong, and the van may belong to a delivery firm. But the same vehicle in the same spot at the same time each day is a pattern worth writing down. The plate number is the clue, and rented cloud addresses are the plate numbers of the internet.
takeaways: Rented cloud servers provide attackers with stable and reputable looking addresses.
Inbound logons from hosting ranges are weak alone but useful with failure counts and account value.
Unexpected compute spending in your own cloud accounts can mean infrastructure is being used against you.

objectives: Explain what a virtual private server is and why adversaries rent rather than compromise one
Identify authentication, flow, and cloud billing telemetry that reveals hosting infrastructure
Score remote access attempts based on hosting provider address ranges and failure counts
Distinguish employee lab spending from infrastructure provisioned for an operation
Interpret hosting address context during an investigation without treating it as proof
dataSources: Remote access authentication logs with source address and result for virtual private network and remote desktop services
Cloud provider billing and cost anomaly reports showing new compute spend by account and service
AWS CloudTrail and Azure Activity log entries for instance creation by unfamiliar identities
Firewall and proxy logs enriched with autonomous system and hosting provider classification
Threat intelligence feeds listing hosting ranges recently associated with malicious activity
logic: The pattern is contact between your environment and commercial hosting infrastructure in a way that does not match business need: repeated remote access attempts from hosting provider address ranges, especially with many failures across several accounts, or new compute instances in your own cloud accounts created by identities and payment profiles with no project history. The fields to correlate are the source address and its autonomous system classification, the target service, the authentication outcome, the calling identity in the cloud audit log, and the cost centre attached to the spend. Benign activity includes staff using a rented server for a lab, contractors connecting from their own cloud environment, and legitimate backup or monitoring services hosted by providers. The malicious case is a cluster of failures, a short lived instance with no billing owner, and a source address seen in recent threat reporting.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Remote Access Attempts From Hosting Provider Ranges
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: security
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 4625
#     LogonType: 10
#   filter:
#     SourceIp|cidr:
#       - '10[.]0[.]0[.]0/8'
#   condition: selection and not filter | count() by SourceIp > 10
# level: medium
falsePositives: Employees running personal lab servers in a commercial cloud and connecting to office services
Contractors and vendors who operate from their own cloud hosted jump hosts
Legitimate software as a service platforms whose backend runs on shared hosting ranges
Approved security testing that originates from a provider hosted testing environment
tuningNotes: Enrich every source address with autonomous system and hosting classification, then baseline which hosting ranges your business actually uses, including vendor platforms, and allowlist those. Require a failure threshold and multiple distinct accounts before alerting on authentication events, and treat a single successful logon from a hosting range as context rather than an incident. Scope the billing rule to accounts with no project tag. Blocking all hosting ranges would break vendor access and remote work, so keep the rule scored and review rather than automatic.
